explanation: No consistent token or context: top examples span units in scientific text (lm W-1, per hour), code punctuation like expect(" and die(', pronouns, prepositions, word-fragments and numerals across technical and news text. Firing can't be predicted from token identity; maybe a loose bias toward mid-sentence tokens in dense technical/scientific prose.

Fires on the verb or word that comes right after a first-person or greeting opener in friendly direct address to readers, most strongly on 'hope' in 'I/We hope you...' (blog sign-offs, website greetings). Weaker on similar intro formulas such as 'my name is', 'This is my first post', 'may I present', 'share with you'. Near zero in neutral text.

Fires on the middle or continuation token of a fixed, highly predictable multi-token name or boilerplate phrase. The clearest case is 'Software' in 'Free Software Foundation' in GPL license headers; others are runat, Rodham, Max-Planck, esri/, badge URLs and BOOST_MPL. The strongest example is a newline after a footnote number in a legal opinion. Weak on ordinary text.

Fires on the 2nd or later subword piece of a rare proper name or identifier where the model has to copy the spelling from earlier context. Typical cases: a surname repeated after its first mention (Over[be]a, Tol[kin], P[rie]be), digits inside citation IDs or strain numbers, and code identifiers repeated from earlier. Weak on common words.

Mixed bag with no shared feature. Includes code and API path segments ('.php' in index.php, '.it', 'Reference', 'categories', '(int)(' casts), 'same-sex', and 'remainder' in math word problems. Most examples are code or technical, but the triggering token varies widely.

Diffuse. Fires on tokens inside lists or names of places and items (commas between place names such as 'Taichung, Taiwan' or 'New South Wales, South Australia', CJK characters in names and strings), code arguments, and articles like 'a' and 'the' in fixed phrases. No single trigger predicts strong firing.

Fires mainly on the return-type keyword at the start of a function or method declaration, above all 'void' after access modifiers like 'private' or 'public static' in C#, Java, C++ or Objective-C, and similar slots such as VB 'Sub', a Go 'var _', or the case label in a switch. Smaller offshoot on the assignment '=' in MATLAB/Octave lines and on mid-word pieces of non-English words. Weak elsewhere.

Fires on verbs or nouns meaning ending, going away, switching off or disbanding (goes, going, gave up, thrown out, subsided, shut down, turned off, disbanded, disclaimed, absence), especially when something fades or stops. Moderate on related motion verbs. Weak elsewhere.

Fires inside words in non-English, non-ASCII text. It is strongest on the first subword of a German noun after an article ('eine Weile', 'einen Antrag', 'Betrag'). It is also strong on byte-fragment tokens inside Japanese and Chinese characters split across tokens. Near zero in English prose.

Fires on function words or punctuation that start a qualifying or continuation clause in the middle of a sentence, such as quantifiers 'every/all/any', 'where', 'per', 'to' in ranges, 'not' in 'are not limited to', and commas before a clause. Also fires on indentation whitespace in code before a statement. Fairly diffuse; context-driven rather than tied to one token.

Fires on tokens in technical or scientific text that continue a known compound term or name (Clauser, Hind III, Banana River, Savannah River, Oceanographic, crystal oscillator). It is also strong on 'Solve' and 'Suppose' and similar command words in templated math problems ('Calculate the greatest common factor of'). The trigger is the predictable next piece of a set phrase.

Fires on a non-initial subword piece inside a proper name or abbreviation, most notably 'ty' in 'Atty.' in legal case listings ('Asst. Atty. Gen.'). Also surnames, place names (Karachi, Krasnooktyabrskoye, Czechów) and terms like 'Actin' and 'photoplethysmography'. Weak on whole common words.

Fires on the first subword of a word that gets split into pieces, often a rare or proper noun or a technical term. Examples include 'py' in pyrolytic, 'cy' in cytochrome, 'mol' in molten, 's' in sapphire, Ka in Kaunas and T in Tangerang. It also fires on 'android:' attribute colons and short variable names (e, tz) at the start of a statement. The common thread is a token where the next piece is predictable.

Fires strongly on '=' in MATLAB/Octave assignment lines after a % comment ('R = roots(...)', '[OUT,OFFS] ='). Everything else is weak (under 40%) and scattered: CJK characters, chemical name fragments, punctuation. Only the MATLAB assignment case gives strong firing.
